bp: A news recommender is deciding what a reader should see at a moment when the world itself is changing. Yesterday's sports habit, month-long interest in technology, or steady preference for local politics may still matter, but today's breaking event can quickly make a different topic feel urgent. The paper serves this ordinary problem: choose news that fits both who the reader has tended to be and what the reader appears to care about now. The input evidence is a history of user-news interactions, represented not only as isolated clicks but as relationships among users and articles over time. The abstract says older systems often rely on one static interaction graph, meaning one frozen map of who touched what. That map can capture stable collaborative patterns, such as users with related histories giving clues about one another, but news requires freshness. This paper asks how to keep the durable map while also reading the reader's recent path in stages.
wh: The hard part is that user interest has two different clocks. Some preferences move slowly: a person may usually read finance, sports, science, or regional news. Other interests move quickly because an election, disaster, product launch, court case, or celebrity story changes what feels relevant. A recommender that forgets long-term history becomes jumpy; it may treat a single accidental click as a new identity. A recommender that trusts only long-term history becomes stale; it may keep showing articles from an old habit after the reader has turned toward a developing story. The abstract names another difficulty: collaborative patterns can be high-order, meaning useful evidence may arrive through indirect relationships in the overall user-item map, not just from one user's own clicks. A single static graph has trouble serving both needs because it mixes old and new interactions into one structure. Once time is collapsed, the system cannot easily tell stable preference from recent movement.
naive: A smart beginner would build one user-article graph from all recorded interactions, learn which users and news articles are close in that graph, and recommend articles near the user's historical neighborhood. This uses the useful idea that readers with related behavior can help predict one another. It fails because the graph is frozen after time has been pooled. A click from weeks ago and a click from this morning may receive similar treatment, even though news value changes quickly. Another beginner solution would look only at the most recent clicks. That adapts faster, but it throws away stable habits and the wider collaborative clues found in the full interaction graph. The paper is trying to avoid both failures: stale memory and shallow recency.
ap: The core idea is to split preference modeling into a global view and a local temporal view, then use both. The global component reads the overall interaction graph to capture long-term collaborative signal: if many related readers and articles form a pattern across the whole history, that pattern should still inform what the user usually values. The local component cuts historical interactions into stage-wise temporal subgraphs, meaning smaller maps for successive time periods. Those staged maps let the model see how recent interest changes rather than treating the whole past as one pile. Inside the local part, one branch follows the progression of recent stages in order, while another branch selectively compares distant moments in the recent history when an earlier stage still matters. The central move is therefore not simply adding time stamps. It creates separate mechanical places for stable preference, recent drift, and longer temporal echoes.
mech: The mechanism starts with user-news interaction records. From all interactions, the global preference component builds or uses the overall interaction graph: users and news articles are places on a map, and an interaction is a link saying that this reader engaged with this article. Learning on this full map gives each user evidence from direct behavior and from collaborative structure, such as related users or articles connected through shared histories. In parallel, the local component partitions the interaction history into ordered stages. Each stage becomes a temporal subgraph, a smaller relationship map describing what interactions were active during that slice of time. The staged sequence then has two paths. The LSTM branch, a sequence model that updates a running memory step by step, reads the stages in order so it can notice progressive movement in recent interests. The self-attention branch, unpacked as selective comparison among stages, lets one stage look back to other stages and assign more influence to the moments that help explain the present, even if they are not immediately adjacent. The outputs of the global and local views are combined into a user preference signal. Candidate news articles are then scored or ranked using that signal, and the system returns recommendations meant to be fresh without discarding stable reading habits.
math: The mathematical objects are a graph, an ordered sequence of subgraphs, and a ranking score. In the graph, nodes are users and news articles, and links are observed interactions. The graph idea fits because one reader's sparse history may be clarified by neighboring readers and articles, but it must be used carefully because links from old events can become stale. The sequence idea appears because the order of interactions changes their meaning. A recent cluster of articles about one developing story is stronger evidence about now than the same articles scattered months apart. The LSTM branch is a learned memory update rule: at each stage it keeps part of the old state, adds part of the new evidence, and produces a revised summary. The selective-comparison branch uses weights over stages, which is a way of asking which earlier moments should count more for the current recommendation. Ranking then compresses all this evidence into scores for candidate articles so a small list can be shown. The main tradeoff is stability versus freshness. The global graph protects stable collaborative evidence; the temporal subgraphs and sequence rules protect recent movement. The risk is that compressing interest into scores can hide why a topic is being promoted.
dots: This paper belongs to the recommender-systems family because it chooses a small set of articles from a much larger pile using partial evidence about a user. It connects to sequence modeling because the user's history is not a bag of clicks; the order and spacing of reading events help define what the next article should be. It connects to network reasoning because the global interaction graph lets evidence travel through user-article relationships instead of relying only on one person's own record. It also connects to ranking because the practical output is an ordered set of candidate news items. Neighboring repo ideas include ONeRec, which treats news recommendation as a path that can steer a reader over time, and GenCI, which separates longer preference from immediate intent for click prediction. The stage-wise news paper takes the temporal recommendation branch: it focuses on how stable collaborative preference and fast topic drift can be represented together.
ww: The approach should work better than the naive static graph when recent behavior contains real signal about a changing news context. A full-history graph can find durable similarities, but it cannot easily tell whether a link is evidence of current interest or only past habit. By slicing history into stages, the model preserves when evidence appeared. The ordered branch can notice direction: if a reader moves from general economy articles to several articles about a current market event, the recent progression matters. The selective-comparison branch helps when the useful earlier clue is not simply the latest one; a story may unfold over several stages, and an older related stage can still explain today's interest. The global component keeps the system from overreacting to one odd click by supplying the user's broader collaborative neighborhood. The combination is sensible because news reading is neither fully stable nor fully momentary. It is a moving preference anchored by habits, and the paper's design gives each part of that structure a separate route into the final score.
po: The payoff is a recommender designed to produce fresher and more relevant news suggestions across different user behaviors and temporal settings. The abstract reports experiments on two large real-world datasets and says the method consistently outperforms strong baselines. In practical terms, the system buys a way to react to emerging events and trending topics without throwing away the long-term reading habits and collaborative patterns that make personalization useful. The result should matter most when a user's recent behavior is meaningful, not random, and when stale recommendations would quickly lose value.
limits: The method assumes that the recorded interaction history is a trustworthy signal of interest. Clicks may reflect headlines, placement, limited exposure, or platform nudges rather than deep preference. The stage partitions also matter: if the time slices are too coarse, short-term changes blur; if too fine, each subgraph may be noisy. The global graph helps only when collaborative neighbors are genuinely informative, and it can also spread popularity bias. The abstract reports stronger results on two large datasets, but it does not prove reliability across all news sites, cultures, cold-start users, unusual breaking events, or long-term effects on reader diversity.
